oil.summary: Crude staged a dramatic weekly rally, with Brent settling at $87.62/bbl (+4.02% on the day, +15.27% on the week) and WTI at $81.31 (+2.98%/+13.85%), as the Strait of Hormuz conflict dominated flow. The US struck an oil tanker with missiles enforcing an Iran blockade, Ukraine hit Russia's last gas refinery, and Gulf neighbors' exports effectively shut while Iranian oil paradoxically continued to move through the strait. Washington simultaneously expanded sanctions targeting the Shamkhani network and signalled potential 100% tariffs on India over Russian oil purchases. South Korea pivoted to the Red Sea route as Hormuz alternatives. Product cracks diverged sharply: RBOB fell 3.12% on the day while heating oil dropped 2.31%, suggesting some demand-side hesitation despite the crude surge. Baker Hughes data showed US rig counts rising this week. China confirmed a domestic gasoline and diesel price hike effective July 18.
drivers: US enforcement of Iran blockade via direct tanker strike and expanded sanctions drives a large geopolitical risk premium into Brent and WTI
Near-halt of Hormuz tanker traffic for Gulf neighbors disrupts physical supply; South Korea, Baghdad, and China all scrambling for alternative routes and long-term supply deals
Product markets (RBOB, heating oil) sold off intraday despite crude strength, signalling possible demand-destruction concerns at elevated price levels

gas.summary: The gas picture splits sharply along geographic lines. TTF surged to 56.305 €/MWh (+2.77% on the day, +15.72% on the week, +34.80% on the month) as European supply anxiety intensified following Ukraine's strike on Russia's last gas refinery and ongoing Hormuz disruptions cutting LNG flows to Europe. Henry Hub, by contrast, slipped on the week to $2.918/MMBtu (-0.75% WoW, -9.91% MoM), reflecting ample domestic US supply buffering the global shock. China's state LNG importers are actively negotiating long-term supply contracts from exporters not reliant on the Strait of Hormuz, a structural demand shift with long-dated implications. The Baker Hughes rig count increase in the US also points to modest supply growth on the Henry Hub side.
drivers: Ukraine strike on Russia's last gas refinery tightens European supply expectations, amplifying the TTF rally
Hormuz disruptions push China to seek non-Hormuz LNG supply, reshaping long-term contract flows globally
Henry Hub remains insulated by domestic US supply abundance, creating a record TTF-HH spread divergence

power.summary: EU carbon (EUA) was largely static, settling at $75.255/EUA (+0.64% on the day, near flat on the week and month), suggesting carbon markets have not yet priced a sustained fuel-switching shock despite TTF's 34.80% monthly surge. The key supply-security storyline is geopolitical: Iran instructed Yemen's Houthis to prepare to disrupt Red Sea shipping if the US strikes Iranian power infrastructure, threatening the last viable tanker alternative to Hormuz and raising broader energy infrastructure risk. New Jersey enacted legislation launching a competitive programme for small modular reactors, adding to nuclear momentum. India proposed stricter CAFE-III vehicle emission rules aimed at cutting oil consumption. EUA inertia despite elevated gas prices is the standout anomaly to watch.
drivers: Iran-directed Houthi threat to Red Sea shipping could close the last major tanker corridor, escalating energy infrastructure risk across all fuels
New Jersey SMR legislation extends the nuclear renaissance to the US Northeast, a long-term structural signal for low-carbon power capacity
EUA flat on the month despite TTF +35% suggests carbon market has not yet reflected potential gas-to-coal switching or supply disruption pass-through — a divergence worth monitoring
